Cox score with rho-gamma weights

Source: R/weightedCox.R
cox_score_rhogamma.Rd

Calculates the Cox score statistic for weighted log-rank tests.

Usage

cox_score_rhogamma(
  beta,
  time,
  delta,
  z,
  w_hat = rep(1, length(time)),
  wt_rg = rep(1, length(time)),
  score_only = TRUE
)

Arguments

beta

Log hazard ratio parameter.

time

Numeric vector of event times.

delta

Numeric vector of event indicators.

z

Numeric vector of group indicators.

w_hat

Numeric vector of weights.

wt_rg

Numeric vector of rho-gamma weights.

score_only

Logical; if TRUE, returns only the score.

Value

Numeric value of the score or, with score_only = FALSE, a list with score, sig2_score (variance of the score at beta), sig2_beta_asy (sig2_score / i_bhat^2), K_wt_rg and i_bhat (the information).

Details

With w_hat absent or all equal, sig2_score and sig2_beta_asy are the formulas used before (score_calculation) and are unchanged. When w_hat is not all equal, sig2_score is the sum of squared per-subject score contributions \(\sum_i \psi_i(\beta)^2\) described below and sig2_beta_asy is that sum over i_bhat^2. The score, K_wt_rg and i_bhat are unchanged. time is taken to be sorted, as df_counting returns it; the time weight of a tied time is the one at its first observation.

Variance of the log-rank and Cox score with subject weights

With no subject weights, or with all subject weights equal, the weighted log-rank test and the weighted Cox estimate are computed as before, and their results are unchanged. When the subject weights are not all equal, the variance of the weighted score is the sum of squared per-subject score contributions, $$\widehat{Var}\{U(\beta)\} = \sum_i \psi_i(\beta)^2,$$ $$\psi_i(\beta) = a_i \Big( D_i K(U_i) \{Z_i - \bar z(U_i, \beta)\} - e^{\beta Z_i} \sum_{s \le U_i} K(s) \{Z_i - \bar z(s, \beta)\} d\hat\Lambda(s, \beta) \Big),$$ where \(U_i\), \(D_i\), \(Z_i\) and \(a_i\) are subject \(i\)'s time, event indicator, arm (0/1) and subject weight, \(K(s)\) is the time weight of the scheme, \(S_0(s, \beta) = \sum_j a_j 1(U_j \ge s) e^{\beta Z_j}\), \(\bar z(s, \beta) = \sum_j a_j 1(U_j \ge s) Z_j e^{\beta Z_j} / S_0(s, \beta)\) and \(d\hat\Lambda(s, \beta) = \sum_j a_j D_j 1(U_j = s) / S_0(s, \beta)\). Sums over \(s\) run over distinct times (events at a tied time are added up), and a term whose \(S_0\) is 0 is 0. The score itself, \(-\sum_i \psi_i(\beta)\), is the one computed before and does not change, and neither does any point estimate. The log-rank z-score is the score at \(\beta = 0\) over \(\sqrt{\sum_i \psi_i(0)^2}\); the variance of the log hazard ratio estimate is \(\sum_i \psi_i(\hat\beta)^2 / i(\hat\beta)^2\) with \(i(\hat\beta)\) the information (unchanged); in a stratified analysis the contributions are computed within each stratum and the score and its variance are sums over strata. For Fleming-Harrington (0, 0) weights this is the robust variance of survival::coxph(weights = w, robust = TRUE, ties = "breslow"): the same robust score test and the same robust standard error. Results no longer depend on how the weights are scaled (weights w, 10 * w and w / sum(w) give the same z-score and standard error). By default the weights are treated as fixed and known. For weights estimated by a logistic propensity model, weight_variance = "estimated" carries their estimation into the test and the intervals (section "Estimated weights"). When the weights are extreme (low effective sample size) the intervals can be too short under either option.
